How to compare business loan offers that are quoted in different ways

A bank quotes an APR. An online lender quotes a monthly rate plus a fee. A cash advance quotes a factor rate. All three can be on your desk in the same week for the same $100,000, and none of them tells you the price in the same unit. The way through is to turn every offer into the same two numbers: the true APR and the dollars it costs.

Open the free comparator

The method

1. Start from the cash you will actually receive

Subtract every fee taken at closing from the headline amount. A $100,000 loan with a 3% origination fee and $2,500 of closing costs puts $94,500 in your account while you still repay $100,000.

2. Write out the payments, not the rate

For a loan, the payment on the full amount at the stated rate. For a factor offer, amount times the factor rate, divided by the number of payments. Note how often payments come out: weekly and daily payments leave the account faster than the monthly equivalent suggests.

3. Solve for the true APR

The true APR is the rate at which the cash you received equals the present value of every payment. It is the one number that lets a factor rate and a term loan sit in the same column. A 1.3 factor over twelve months is over 50% APR; the same 1.3 over six months is more than double that.

4. Put the dollars next to the rate

The lowest APR on the longest term often costs the most dollars. Look at total repaid minus cash received and at the cost for each dollar you receive, then decide which matters for what the money is for.

5. Test the payment against a bad month

Compare the monthly outflow with your revenue and with the cash flow you have left for debt service. A payment that is fine on average and not in your slowest month is the one that causes trouble.

6. Ask what early repayment does

A loan usually returns unearned interest, less any penalty. A fixed-payback advance usually does not. If you expect to repay early, enter the month and see which offer changes most.

A worked example

Four invented offers on $100,000: a five-year bank loan at 9.5% with 1% plus $500 of fees, a ten-year SBA-style loan at 11% with 3.5% plus $2,500 in fees, a two-year online loan at 22% with 4% fees and weekly payments, and a nine-month cash advance at a 1.32 factor with daily payments. The bank loan has the lowest true APR; the ten-year loan costs the most in dollars despite a lower APR than the online loan; the advance is several times the APR of any of them.

Try it with your own offers

Questions

What is the difference between APR and a factor rate?

An APR is an annual rate charged on the balance you still owe, so it falls as you repay. A factor rate is a one-time multiplier on the amount: 1.3 on $100,000 is $30,000 of cost however fast you repay. Convert the factor offer to an APR using the real payment schedule to compare it with a loan.

What fees should I include when comparing offers?

Every fee taken out of the amount or added to the payments: origination, packaging, underwriting, guarantee and closing fees. Include them all; the tool treats them as reductions of the cash you receive, which is how they raise the true APR.

Should I always choose the lowest APR?

Not automatically. The lowest APR on a long term can cost the most dollars. Choose by what the money will earn: if it will pay back within the term at a rate above the APR, a more expensive but faster or easier-to-get offer can still be worth it.

Rules, fees and rates vary and change; check current guidance or ask a qualified adviser. Figures in the example are invented.

BUSINESS LOAN OFFER COMPARATOR · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER · NOTHING UPLOADED

Four financing offers, four different ways of quoting the price. Compare them honestly.

Type in each offer you have received — a bank term loan, an SBA-style loan, an online lender, a merchant cash advance — and get the true APR after fees, the cash that actually reaches your account, total repaid, the cost per dollar received, and what paying early would do, ranked side by side. A factor rate of 1.3 and a 22% APR stop being impossible to compare.

Your figures never leave this browser tab. Planning aid, not legal, tax, or financial advice. It does not know your credit, collateral or any lender's real terms. See how to compare business loan offers for the method.

The offers

kind is loan (rate is an APR such as 9.5) or factor (rate is a factor rate such as 1.32). Only the first five columns are needed. Fee % and flat fees come out of the cash you receive. Payments per year: 12 monthly, 26 biweekly, 52 weekly, 252 business-daily. The last column is the prepayment penalty on a loan, or the discount a factor lender gives for early payoff (usually 0). Lines starting with # are ignored.

Enter your offers, then click the button.

Things to check

How it is calculated

Cash received is the amount minus the percentage and flat fees. Payment for a loan is the standard level payment on the full amount at the stated APR; for a factor offer it is amount × factor rate spread evenly over the payments in the term. True APR is the internal rate of return of the whole stream: the cash you get at the start against every payment you make, found by bisection, then multiplied by payments per year. Effective annual rate compounds that period rate over a year. Cost of money is total repaid minus cash received, so fees count. Early payoff uses the loan's outstanding balance plus any prepayment percentage, and for a factor offer the unpaid remainder less any discount you enter.

Not modelled: variable rates, interest-only periods and balloons, a line of credit's drawdowns, personal guarantees, collateral, covenants, tax treatment, and any lender's actual fee schedule (including SBA guarantee and servicing fees, which you enter as the percentages on your term sheet). Unverified: checked against textbook payment formulas and invented offers in unit tests, not against a real lender's disclosure; a lender's own APR disclosure can differ because of its own assumptions, and the agreement governs.

Common questions

How do I compare a business loan with a merchant cash advance?

Convert both to the same yardstick, the annual percentage rate you actually pay on the cash you actually receive. Enter the amount, the rate (an APR for a loan, a factor rate such as 1.3 for an advance), the payback term, the fees and how often payments come out. The tool solves for the true APR including fees, so a 1.3 factor over nine months and a 22% loan with a 4% fee can be set side by side.

What is a factor rate and how do I turn it into an APR?

A factor rate is a multiplier on the amount: 1.3 on $100,000 means you repay $130,000 in total, whatever the time it takes. Because the cost is fixed, the shorter the payback the higher the APR. Enter the factor rate and the number of months you expect to take and the tool computes the APR from the actual payment stream.

Why is the true APR higher than the rate the lender quoted?

Because fees are taken out of the cash you receive but you still repay the full amount. Borrowing $100,000 with a 3% origination fee puts $97,000 in your account while the payments are calculated on $100,000, so you pay the quoted rate on money you never got. The tool takes the fees off the cash received before it solves for the rate.

Is the cheapest APR always the cheapest offer?

No. A ten-year loan at 8% can have a lower APR than a two-year loan at 14% and still cost far more dollars in total, because you owe it for longer. The tool shows both the APR and the dollars of cost, and what each costs per dollar you receive, so you can pick the one that fits what the money will earn.

What happens if I pay the loan off early?

Amortizing loans give back the interest you have not yet incurred, less any prepayment fee, so paying off early usually lowers the dollars you pay but can raise the effective APR if there is a penalty. Fixed-payback advances usually give no discount, so the cost stays the same however early you repay. Enter a payoff month and a prepayment percentage to see both.

Does this tell me which lender to pick or whether I qualify?

No. It does arithmetic on the offers you type in. It does not know your credit, collateral, personal guarantee, covenants, current SBA fee schedules or any lender's terms, and it does not recommend a lender. Read the agreement and ask a qualified adviser before you sign.

Is my financial information uploaded anywhere?

No. The offers and revenue figures you enter are read and calculated in this browser tab. Nothing is sent to a server and the tool does not store your offers. It works offline once the page has loaded.
